summary:
Satellites detect heat sources across the planet every day: wildfires, but also agricultural and waste burning. Stitch the MODIS and VIIRS records together, however, and the world's burning activity appears to jump fourfold in 2012. It did not; the sensor changed. VIIRS sees smaller fires than MODIS, so raw records from 2000 to today cannot be compared.

We built FireBridge, a machine-learning harmonizer trained on the 14 years both sensors observed together (2012–2025). It converts every MODIS detection since 2000 into what VIIRS S-NPP would have counted, and bridges to NOAA-20 after S-NPP ended on 2 November 2026. The result is one consistent record of satellite fire detections from November 2000 to today, worldwide at 0.1° and for 5,051 regions.

We then asked who would use this record: wildfire and emergency responders, land managers and scientists. Our web app gives them what they need: a year-by-month burning calendar, this month compared with the regional historical median, CSV export, and FireOutlook, which estimates detections for the next day, the next 30 days and up to 12 months ahead. Every number is validated on years the models never saw.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Satellites detect heat sources every day: wildfires, agricultural and waste burning, and other combustion. We started from this data and asked who would look at it. Wildfire and emergency responders, early-warning staff, land managers and scientists each need the same record but ask different questions, so we designed a website where they can take exactly what they need. For a fire manager the two questions are: "Is burning activity this month higher than usual?" and "What about the next 30 days?"

The project has two parts.

1) Harmonization (FireBridge). MODIS (1 km pixels, since 2000) and VIIRS (375 m pixels, since 2012) count the same fire differently: worldwide, VIIRS S-NPP records about 4.4 times as many detections as MODIS over the same 2012–2025 period (2.6 times in Korea). FireBridge expresses every period as "detections VIIRS S-NPP would have recorded":

- 2000-11 to 2002-06: Terra-only MODIS, converted by FireBridge-Terra

- 2002-07 to 2012-01: Aqua+Terra MODIS, converted by FireBridge

- 2012-02 to 2026-11-02: VIIRS S-NPP observations as they are

- From 2026-11-03: NOAA-20 x 1.013 (ratio learned from 8 overlapping years), NOAA-21 as a backup

Only one reference satellite produces each value, so adding satellites never inflates the record.

2) Web app. Users select a country, province or district, or draw a box or polygon, and see:

- a year-by-month burning activity calendar (2000 to today) with an accessible color ramp

- the current month against the historical median of the same month (percentile, ratio, "above / normal / below usual")

- point and cell maps, daily views, CSV download of harmonized detections

- FireOutlook: next-day spread probability (Korea, Argentina), next-month occurrence probability, and a 30-day outlook with daily probabilities, expected detections and a 10–90% range

- context layers: Fire Weather Index (Canadian FWI system), detection events and burned area, burning regime (large fires vs. many small burns)

HOW IT WORKS

- Data cleaning: vegetation-fire detections only (type 0), exclusion of 90,959 persistent industrial/volcanic 0.01° cells, satellite-status checks so "no data" is never shown as "no detections".

- FireBridge: gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost, GPU) with a Tweedie loss suited to zero-heavy counts. 24 inputs per 0.1° cell-month: Aqua/Terra detections, active days, confidence, fire radiative power, night share, 3x3 neighbors, season, location, Terra orbit drift, country and continent. A quantile model provides a 10–90% uncertainty band.

- Point-level consistency: every detection carries a harmonized weight, so points, cells and regional totals always add up (zero mismatches across the archive).

- FireOutlook: direct multi-horizon models (one model per lead time instead of feeding predictions back recursively, which accumulates error), LightGBM+XGBoost ensembles, district-level models, AutoTheta/AutoETS for continental and global counts, and calibration so a "30%" really happens about 30% of the time. Where a model cannot beat the historical baseline, the app shows the baseline and says so.

- Updates: NASA FIRMS near-real-time data are ingested daily and harmonized with the same rules.

VALIDATION (models are always tested on years they never saw)

- FireBridge, leave-one-year-out 2012–2025: total ratio 0.992 globally, 0.986 in Korea and Argentina; monthly correlation 0.995 globally, 0.97 in Korea; Korean monthly error halved versus a simple ratio (MAE 80 to 42); the 10–90% band covers about 80% of observations.

- Self-check of the 2012 sensor boundary, using MODIS itself as a constant reference: passed globally and in Argentina. In Korea we found pre-2012 values about 30% too high, so the "compared with usual" verdict now uses a VIIRS-era baseline wherever the check fails (Korea's recent "below usual" share fell from 53% to 33%).

- Leave-continent-out test reported openly: FireBridge does not transfer to unseen continents, so the released dataset is trained on all regions.

- FireOutlook, 2024–2025 holdout: next-day skill +16% over climatology, +10% at 7 days, +7.7% next month, still +4.4% at 12 months; global monthly detection counts 11.6% error vs. 27.1% for the historical median. For the 30-day outlook, regional probabilities are calibrated so the average forecast matches observed frequency.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

- Wildfire and emergency responders and early-warning staff can see when a region's burning season peaks, whether this month is unusual, and where the next 30 days need attention. The March 2025 wildfires in southeastern Korea appear as the highest month in 26 years, and 92% of large wildfires (100 ha or more) in Korea Forest Service records were detected by satellite.

- Scientists get a 26-year, sensor-consistent record with uncertainty, open code and a SHA-256-verified data release.

- Land managers can separate agricultural burning from large fires and find recurring burn sites.

- The method survives satellite turnover: when S-NPP ended on 2 November 2026, the record continued the next day through NOAA-20.

TOOLS

Python, Polars, PyArrow, XGBoost (GPU), LightGBM, scikit-learn, statsforecast, Shapely, pyproj, uv; web app frontend in TypeScript and backend in Java; GitHub Releases for data distribution.
